Leadership Reflection:
Then vs. Now

A retrospective on the growth between my earlier portfolio and my leadership practice today.

What Still Represents Me

The throughline of ownership and craft — leading QA automation across enterprise systems at AT&T/DirecTV and State Farm, and driving community-scale work like the California Digital Twins Hub, I still lead by getting close to the problem, holding a high technical bar, and owning outcomes, not just tasks.

What Feels Outdated

My earlier portfolio framed leadership mostly as technical execution and individual expertise. It underrepresented the collaborative, cross-functional, and cross-cultural work I now do daily — translating between engineering, design, policy, and community stakeholders.

How I'm Changing

I'm shifting from being the most capable individual contributor to multiplying capability in others and in systems — through documentation that outlasts a project, mentoring via code review, and treating resilience as the true measure of leadership.

Strengths Profile

Results and reflection from my strengths assessment, including where reliance becomes risk.
Top Strengths
  1. Analytical Rigor & Attention to Detail
    A QA-trained instinct for finding edge cases and failure points before they become problems.
  2. Ownership & Reliability
    Following work through to completion and being the person a team can hand ambiguity to.
  3. Cross-Cultural & Cross-Functional Communication
    Bilingual (English/Farsi) fluency and comfort translating between engineering, design, and community stakeholders.
  4. Craft & Aesthetic Sensibility
    A high, self-imposed bar for polish and coherence in anything shipped — from test suites to visual design.
Reflection: Reliance, Overuse & Blind Spots

My top strengths are analytical rigor, ownership, cross-cultural communication, and craft — and of these, the one I rely on most is analytical rigor: the QA-honed habit of interrogating a system until I understand every way it could fail. That same strength becomes a limitation when it tips into over-verification — spending disproportionate time hardening something already good enough, delaying delivery to chase one more edge case, or defaulting to checking things myself instead of delegating that judgment. Recognizing this overuse pattern is pushing me toward setting explicit "good enough" thresholds, timeboxing quality passes, and treating delegation of judgment — not just tasks — as its own leadership skill to build.

Personality & Communication

How my personality shapes the way I work with people and communicate as a leader.
Reflection

The parts of my personality results that feel most accurate are being analytical, dependable, and focused on details. I naturally like to understand a problem before making a decision, and I take ownership when something needs to get done. At the same time, I question the idea that being detail-oriented means I always need more information before acting. I have learned that leadership sometimes requires making a reasonable decision without having every answer. My personality also affects how I communicate because I usually try to be clear, organized, and direct. I listen carefully and want people to understand the reason behind a decision, but I am also working on being more flexible and adjusting my communication style depending on the person and situation.

Leadership Style Analysis

How my leadership is moving from individual execution toward helping others succeed.
Reflection

My leadership style reflects both how I lead now and the kind of leader I want to become. I tend to lead through responsibility, problem solving, and being willing to step in when the team needs support, but I am learning that leadership is not about doing everything myself. A good example is when I work on technical or project-based tasks and notice an issue that could affect the final result. My first instinct is usually to investigate it myself, but I have become more intentional about sharing what I know, documenting the process, and giving other people room to make decisions. That shift shows me that I am moving from proving what I can do individually to helping the whole team become stronger.

Leadership Message

Clear communication, trust, and presence.
Reflection

A leader’s communication is effective when people understand the message, know why it matters, and feel comfortable asking questions or sharing a different point of view. I usually communicate my ideas by explaining the problem, giving the important details, and then focusing on the next steps. Because of my technical background, I sometimes include more detail than people actually need. One way I can improve my leadership presence is to make my message simpler and more confident by leading with the main point first, then adding details only when they help. I also want to pay more attention to my tone, body language, and how well I am listening instead of focusing only on what I want to say.

My Leadership Message
“I want to lead by creating clarity, earning trust, and helping people do their best work. I do not need to have every answer, but I do need to listen, take responsibility, communicate clearly, and help the team move forward.”

Leadership Portfolio Artifact · Change Reflection

Learning From What Did Not Work

A reflection on setbacks, response, and change.
Change Reflection

There have been times when a project or task did not go the way I expected, especially when I spent too much time trying to make every detail perfect before moving forward. In those moments, my response was usually to work harder, double-check everything, and try to solve the problem myself. I learned that being responsible is a strength, but overchecking can slow progress and make it harder to delegate. If I faced the same situation now, I would communicate the issue earlier, decide what level of quality is actually needed, ask for input when necessary, and give other team members more ownership. As a leader, I am learning that responding well to change is not about controlling every outcome; it is about staying calm, adapting, and helping the team keep moving.

Creative Leadership Statement

The kind of leader I am becoming.
Final Reflection

My understanding of leadership has changed from thinking mostly about expertise and getting results to understanding that leadership is also about trust, communication, accountability, and helping other people grow. Throughout the course, I noticed a pattern in myself: I take ownership quickly, I care about quality, and I naturally look for problems before they become bigger, but I can also take on too much or spend too much time checking details. I am becoming a leader who still values high standards but understands that strong leadership is not about being the person who does everything. It is about creating clarity, sharing responsibility, listening to different perspectives, and building an environment where people can contribute with confidence.

Creative Leadership Statement
I lead with ownership, curiosity, and respect. My goal is to make difficult problems clearer, build trust through consistent actions, and create space for other people to grow. Success is not only what I accomplish myself; it is what the team is able to accomplish together.
